items.title: What is IaC?
items.text:
Infrastructure as Code (IaC) means provisioning and managing infrastructure using code, instead of manually creating resources via a cloud console (clicks, drag & drop).

In IaC:

  • Infrastructure is defined declaratively
  • The same code can create, update, or destroy resources
  • Infrastructure becomes repeatable and predictable

items.title: Traditional vs IaC
items.text:
graph LR
A[Manual Cloud Console
Click / Drag / Drop] -->|Human Actions| B[Infrastructure]

C[Infrastructure Code
Terraform / ARM / CloudFormation] -->|Automated| D[Infrastructure]

items.title: Why Do We Use Infrastructure as Code?
"Why write code when we can just use the cloud console?"
items.text:
Manual provisioning works fine for:

  • Personal projects
  • Learning or experiments

But it does not scale.

items.title: Example: Three-Tier Application
items.text:
Assume provisioning infra for:

  • Load Balancer
  • Application Servers
  • Database

Time taken manually: ~2 hours

graph TD
LB[Load Balancer] --> APP[Application Servers]
APP --> DB[Database]

That’s acceptable for one environment.

items.title: Multiple Environments Problem
items.text:
In a company, you usually have:

  • Dev
  • QA
  • Staging
  • Production

Manual provisioning time:

Environments Time 1 2 hrs 4 8 hrs 
graph LR
Dev --> QA --> Staging --> Prod

Now imagine:

  • Hundreds of servers
  • Multiple regions
  • Multiple teams

Manual setup becomes:

  • Slow
  • Error-prone
  • Hard to maintain

items.title: Real-World Challenges Without IaC
items.text:
❌ Hard to decommission infra → High cloud cost ❌ Environments differ → "Works on my machine" issue ❌ No easy rollback ❌ No visibility into changes ❌ Security & compliance risks 

graph TD
Manual[Manual Infra] --> Errors[Human Errors]
Manual --> Cost[High Cost]
Manual --> Drift[Environment Drift]

items.title: Key Advantages
items.text:
• Consistent environments across Dev / QA / Prod
  • Write once, deploy many (single codebase)
  • Faster provisioning
  • Reduced human error
  • Cost savings via automation
  • Version control (Git tracks infra changes)
  • Automated cleanup & scheduled destruction
  • Easy to create identical production-like environments
  • Developers can focus on application development
graph LR
Code[Infra Code] --> Repeatable[Repeatable Infra]
Code --> Secure[Secure & Auditable]
Code --> Fast[Fast Provisioning]
Code --> Cheap[Cost Optimized]

items.title: What is a Terraform Provider?
items.text:
A Terraform provider is a plugin that allows Terraform to interact with cloud platforms, SaaS services, or any third-party APIs to provision and manage infrastructure.

Providers are responsible for: - Authenticating with the target platform - Translating Terraform configurations into API calls - Managing the lifecycle of resources (create, read, update, delete)

items.title: High-level Architecture
items.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Terraform Core] --> B[Terraform Registry]
    A --> C[Provider Plugin]
    C --> D[Cloud / Third-Party APIs]

items.title: Terraform Core Version vs Provider Version
items.text:
• Terraform Core

  • The Terraform CLI and engine

  • Handles state management, dependency graph, and execution plan

  • Provider

  • Independent plugins maintained separately

  • Each provider has its own version lifecycle
  • Must be compatible with the Terraform Core version

Terraform Core and Providers are versioned independently, but compatibility matters.

items.title: Why Provider Version Matters
items.text:
Using correct provider versions ensures:

  • Stability and predictable behavior
  • Access to new resources and features
  • Bug fixes and security patches
  • Avoidance of breaking changes

Problems caused by incorrect versions:

  • Breaking schema changes
  • Deprecated or removed resources
  • Incompatible APIs
  • Failed plans or applies

items.title: Version Constraints in Terraform
items.text: Terraform allows you to restrict provider versions using version constraints.

items.title: Common Version Operators
items.text: Operator Meaning = Exact version != Exclude a version > Greater than >= Greater than or equal < Less than <= Less than or equal ~> Pessimistic constraint (recommended)

items.title: Example: Provider Version Constraint
items.text:
terraform {
  required_providers {
    aws = {
      source  = "hashicorp/aws"
      version = "~> 5.0"
    }
  }
}

🔹 ~> 5.0 allows:

  • 5.0.x, 5.1.x, 5.9.x
  • ❌ Not 6.0.0

items.title: Best Practices
items.text:
• Always pin provider versions
  • Use ~> for safe upgrades
  • Lock versions using terraform.lock.hcl
  • Test provider upgrades in non-production environments
  • Track provider changelogs before upgrading

items.title: What is Terraform?
items.text:
Terraform is an Infrastructure as Code (IaC) tool developed by HashiCorp.

It allows you to:

  • Define infrastructure using declarative configuration files
  • Provision resources across multiple cloud platforms
  • Create, update, and destroy infrastructure safely and consistently

Terraform supports many providers, including:

  • AWS
  • Azure
  • Google Cloud Platform (GCP)
  • Kubernetes
  • Various SaaS platforms

items.title: Terraform Provider Ecosystem
items.text:
flowchart TB
    subgraph Terraform
        TF[Terraform Core]
    end

    subgraph Cloud_Providers[Cloud Providers]
        AWS[AWS]
        AZURE[Azure]
        GCP[GCP]
        K8S[Kubernetes]
    end

    TF --> AWS
    TF --> AZURE
    TF --> GCP
    TF --> K8S

Terraform Core uses providers as plugins to interact with different platforms and services.

items.title: How Terraform Works
items.text:
Terraform follows a simple workflow where infrastructure is driven by code.

flowchart LR
    TF_FILES["Terraform Files (.tf)"]
    CLI["Terraform CLI"]
    PROVIDER["Provider Plugin"]
    API["Cloud API"]
    INFRA["Infrastructure Resources"]

    TF_FILES --> CLI
    CLI --> PROVIDER
    PROVIDER --> API
    API --> INFRA

Providers translate Terraform configurations into API calls that create or manage real infrastructure.

items.title: Terraform Lifecycle Phases
items.text:
Terraform operations follow a well-defined execution lifecycle.

flowchart LR
    INIT[terraform init]
    VALIDATE[terraform validate]
    PLAN[terraform plan]
    APPLY[terraform apply]
    DESTROY[terraform destroy]

    INIT --> VALIDATE
    VALIDATE --> PLAN
    PLAN --> APPLY
    APPLY --> DESTROY

items.title: Phase Breakdown
items.text:
• init Initializes the working directory and downloads required providers

  • validate Checks configuration syntax and internal consistency

  • plan Displays the execution plan showing what changes Terraform will make

  • apply Creates or updates infrastructure resources

  • destroy Safely removes all resources managed by Terraform
